title: Why Hotels Skip the 13th Floor (It's Still There)

thumbnail.plane: interior of a luxury hotel elevator lobby at night, polished brass elevator doors closed, marble floor, one warm spotlight, empty, ominous, symmetrical

shots.vo: You step into a hotel elevator and press fourteen. But you are not going to the fourteenth floor.
shots.prompt: close-up of a man's finger pressing a glowing brass button on a hotel elevator panel, mirrored walls, warm light, no numbers visible

shots.vo: Look closely. Twelve. Fourteen. Something is missing.
Thirteen floors up, there is a floor that officially does not exist. Thousands of buildings have one. Maybe the one you slept in last night.
shots.prompt: a long empty hotel corridor at night, rows of closed doors, patterned carpet, one flickering ceiling light, eerie, symmetrical

shots.vo: Why would the most modern buildings on Earth pretend a floor is not there? And who decided it?
shots.prompt: low angle view of a tall glass hotel skyscraper at dusk, rows of lit windows, dramatic sky

shots.vo: Most of us never notice. We step in, press a button, and stare at our phones.
shots.prompt: people waiting in front of hotel elevators in a bright lobby, one looking at a phone, backs to camera, warm light

shots.vo: But in two thousand two, an executive at Otis, one of the biggest elevator makers in the world, estimated that around eighty-five percent of their tall buildings had no button marked thirteen.
Not because of engineering. Because of fear.
shots.prompt: a skyscraper blueprint spread on a wooden desk, pencil and ruler, a desk lamp casting a pool of light, dark office

shots.vo: The fear of thirteen is ancient. At the Last Supper, thirteen sat at the table. One of them was the man who betrayed Jesus.
shots.prompt: a long candlelit wooden table in a stone hall with thirteen robed figures seated along one side, renaissance oil painting style, seen from the end of the table

shots.vo: In Norse mythology, twelve gods sat down to feast. The trickster Loki arrived uninvited, the thirteenth guest. By the end of the night, the beloved god Balder was dead.
shots.prompt: a dark viking feast hall with a long fire pit, twelve figures at a table, a hooded uninvited figure stepping through the great doors, ominous firelight

shots.vo: Over centuries, the story hardened into a rule. Thirteen brings death.
shots.prompt: a narrow medieval village street at dusk, a black cat on cobblestones in the foreground, lanterns, fog

shots.vo: By the eighteen eighties, the fear was so common in New York that a group of men decided to mock it.
shots.prompt: a New York City street in the 1880s at night, gas lamps, horse-drawn carriages, brick buildings, fog

shots.vo: They called themselves the Thirteen Club. Thirteen men at one table. They walked under ladders, spilled salt on purpose, and ate lobster salad moulded into coffins.
shots.prompt: a Victorian dinner party, thirteen men in black suits around a candlelit table, a silver platter in the center holding lobster salad shaped like a small coffin, 1880s

shots.vo: They wanted to prove the fear was nonsense. Did they win?
shots.prompt: a Victorian gentleman in a black suit raising a wine glass and laughing at a candlelit dinner table, seen from the side, face in shadow

shots.vo: No. Because at the very same time, something new was rising over American cities. Skyscrapers.
shots.prompt: New York City in the 1890s, early skyscrapers under construction, steel frames and cranes against a smoky sky, workers on beams

shots.vo: For the first time, buildings climbed past thirteen floors. And the men who built them had a problem.
shots.prompt: a 1900s property developer in a dark suit and bowler hat standing in the street looking up at a tall new office building, back view

shots.vo: Who would rent an office, or buy a home, on the unluckiest floor in the building? If even a few tenants said no, that floor became a loss.
shots.prompt: an empty vacant office floor in an early 1900s building, bare wooden floorboards, dust in sunbeams from tall windows

shots.vo: So they did something very simple. They changed the number.
shots.prompt: close-up of an early 1900s gentleman's hand signing a contract with a fountain pen on a leather desk, lamp light

shots.vo: But here is the catch. The thirteenth floor never disappeared. Count the floors yourself.
The floor labelled fourteen is the thirteenth floor. If you stay there, you are sleeping on it. The number changed. The building did not.
Some buildings hide it as a machine floor, full of pipes and pumps. Some call it twelve A. Most just skip the number, and hope you never count.
shots.prompt: a dim mechanical floor inside a skyscraper, large pipes, pumps and ducts, industrial lights, concrete walls

shots.vo: And it is not only thirteen. In Chinese, the word for four sounds almost like the word for death. Some towers skip every floor with a four in it.
In buildings like that, the number at the top of the panel is higher than the real number of floors.
shots.prompt: a very tall glass tower in a dense Asian city skyline at night, neon reflections, mist

shots.vo: So why does it still happen today? Not because architects believe in bad luck.
shots.prompt: a modern architect's studio with a white scale model of a skyscraper on a table, soft daylight

shots.vo: Because guests do. Hotels say some guests ask to change rooms when they are given one on thirteen.
shots.prompt: a hotel guest with a suitcase at a marble reception desk, the receptionist handing over a key card, warm lobby light, faces not visible

shots.vo: And no developer wants to spend millions on a floor that people are afraid of.
shots.prompt: a skyscraper at night where every floor is lit except one completely dark floor in the middle

shots.vo: So the next time you press fourteen, you will know the truth.
shots.prompt: hotel elevator doors sliding open onto a bright modern corridor, view from inside the elevator

shots.vo: Thirteen is still there. It just goes by a different name.
A floor of steel and concrete, hidden by a two thousand year old fear.
shots.prompt: a quiet hotel corridor at night with one door slightly open and warm light spilling out, mysterious

shots.vo: And that is the hidden why.
shots.prompt: a single round elevator call button glowing amber in a dark wall, close-up, no numbers

shots.vo: Next time: why is Coca-Cola red? The real reason will surprise you. Subscribe, so you don't miss it.
shots.prompt: a plain red soda can standing on a dark wooden table, a single dramatic light, no logo, no text
